newsitem.title: USA: United pilots leave company task forces in protest.
newsitem.headline: United pilots leave company task forces in protest.

text.p: Pilots for United Airlines are withdrawing from company task forces and may soon begin to refuse to fly overtime, as a dispute over wage and contract issues continues, a union spokesman said Tuesday.
"We're going to have them stand down for a while," said Kevin Dohm, a spokesman for the Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA) United Master Executive Council.
The pilots will stand down, or refuse to participate in non-essential task forces, until further notice, Dohm said.
Pilots will continue to serve on essential task forces dealing with air safety and scheduling, Dohm added.

The ALPA, which turned down a mid-term wage increase earlier this month, likely will begin refusing to fly overtime, Dohm said. He added that many United pilots, because of staff shortages, have been flying overtime at straight-pay rates.
"That's one of the items that pilots will have to decide for themselves," Dohm said. "But I imagine all the overtime flying is going to come to a grinding halt."
In a statement, Gerald Greenwald, chairman of United's parent UAL Corp., said he was "extremely disappointed" by the pilots' actions.

"Regardless of what ALPA has been saying, it's clear that the issues raised by the ALPA (Master Executive Council) fundamentally are not about United's culture," Greenwald said. "Instead, they focus on money and their post-ESOP compensation."
Under an employee stock ownership plan (ESOP) put in place over two years ago, the pilots, machinists and salaried employees own a majority of UAL Corp. United is the nation's largest airline.
"Nevertheless, these issues are legitimate and important and deserve -- and will receive -- our priority attention," Greenwald said.
Earlier this month, ALPA rejected United's wage offer with 80 percent voting against a tentative accord. The wage issue now goes to binding arbitration, which must be completed by April 30.

Earlier, UAL, said it earned $20 million, or 12 cents a share, in the fourth quarter, excluding one-time charges, compared with a loss of $18 million, or 58 cents a share, in the 1995 quarter. Revenues grew 8 percent to $3.98 billion from $3.67 billion.
